title: RC Circuits
short: A capacitor charges through a resistor with time constant τ = RC, and once full it blocks steady current.
trouble: Students think an empty capacitor blocks current the moment the switch closes, when at first it acts like a plain wire.

blocks.html: Put a resistor and a capacitor in a loop with a battery and the current changes with time: large at first, then fading away as the capacitor fills. The loop rule explains it, and the answer is the exponential decay you know from algebra, with the capacitance setting the clock.

The loop rule says $\varepsilon = IR + \dfrac{q}{C}$ at every moment. At the start $q = 0$, so $I = \varepsilon/R$: the empty capacitor acts like a plain wire. As charge builds, the capacitor's voltage $q/C$ pushes back, so less voltage is left for the resistor and the current drops. The charging rate is proportional to how far the capacitor still has to go, so the gap shrinks by the same fraction in each equal time: exponential decay, with time constant $\tau = RC$.

$\tau = RC$. Charging: $V_C = \varepsilon\left(1 - e^{-t/RC}\right)$, $I = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{R}e^{-t/RC}$. Discharging: $V_C = V_0e^{-t/RC}$. At $t = 0$ an empty capacitor acts like a wire; after many $\tau$ a full capacitor blocks steady current.

opts.task: Watch the current start at its largest value and fade as the capacitor's voltage rises.

blocks.cap: An RC circuit with $\tau = RC = 1\,\text{s}$. Build one in the Circuit Builder.

blocks.title: Time constant and first current
blocks.q: A $10\,\text{k}\Omega$ resistor, a $100\,\mu\text{F}$ capacitor (empty) and a $9.0\,\text{V}$ battery are switched into a loop. Find $\tau$ and the starting current.
steps: At $t = 0$ the capacitor acts like a wire: $I_0 = \dfrac{9.0\,\text{V}}{10{,}000\,\Omega} = 0.90\,\text{mA}$.

blocks.title: Partly charged
blocks.q: In the same circuit, what is the capacitor's voltage after $2.0\,\text{s}$?

blocks.title: Early and late
blocks.q: A $12\,\text{V}$ battery drives $R_1 = 4\,\Omega$ in series with $R_2 = 8\,\Omega$, and an empty capacitor sits in parallel with $R_2$. Find the current through $R_1$ just after closing the switch and a long time later.
steps: Just after: the empty capacitor acts like a wire across $R_2$, so only $R_1$ limits the current: $I = 12/4 = 3.0\,\text{A}$.
Long after: the full capacitor passes no current, so $R_1$ and $R_2$ are in series: $I = 12/12 = 1.0\,\text{A}$.

blocks.html: Thinking an empty capacitor blocks current the moment the switch closes. It does the opposite: with no charge it has no voltage, so at first it acts like a plain wire and the current is largest. Only once it is full does it act like a break. Check: use $\varepsilon = IR + q/C$ at the moment in question.
